14550:
Show means to make something perceptible — to bring something from a state where it is hidden, unknown, or unnoticed into a state where it can be seen, understood, or felt.

This can be literal (you hold up an object for someone to see) or figurative (you make an idea clear through evidence). But the core remains the same: something becomes visible, evident, or knowable because of the act of showing.

1. To make something visible — to let someone see it

This is the most basic meaning. You take something and put it where someone can see it.

  • She showed me her new ring. (She held it up / presented it to me.)
  • Please show me your passport.
  • He showed me his scar.

The key idea is intentional presentation — you are actively making something available for another person to see.

2. To demonstrate or explain by doing

Here, "show" means to teach someone something — not through words alone, but by actually doing it in front of them so they can watch how it's done.

  • Let me show you how to make coffee. (I'll do it; you watch.)
  • She showed him how to change a tire.
  • He showed us the right way to hold a golf club.

This meaning is incredibly important in everyday life. The difference between telling and showing: telling = describing in words; showing = demonstrating in action. "Let me show you" is an offer to demonstrate.

3. To point to or indicate something

Here, "show" means to direct someone's attention toward something — to point to it or guide them to it.

  • Can you show me where the library is?
  • The map shows the location of the hospital.
  • He showed me the error in her argument. (He pointed it out / drew my attention to it.)

The person or thing doing the "showing" acts as a guide — directing you toward something you couldn't find or see on your own.

4. To prove or demonstrate through evidence

This is a more intellectual use. "Show" here means to make something clear through evidence, data, logic, or results — to prove something.

  • The research shows that smoking causes cancer. (The evidence makes it clear.)
  • She showed that the defendant was lying.
  • The numbers show a clear improvement.

Importantly, when "show" is used this way, it implies the proof is solid and visible in the evidence itself — not just an opinion. If a scientist says "the data shows X," they mean the data itself, as you can see it, makes X undeniable.

5. To display a quality, emotion, or state

You can "show" something that is not a physical object — a feeling, a quality, a characteristic. This means to let that quality become visible in your behaviour or appearance.

  • She showed great patience with the students. (Her patience was visible in her actions.)
  • He showed no sign of fear. (No fear was evident.)
  • The child showed signs of improvement.
  • His exhaustion is starting to show. (It's becoming noticeable in his appearance.)

The idea here is that something internal (an emotion, a quality) becomes externally visible.

6. To be or become visible — without anyone actively doing it

Sometimes things "show" on their own — they become visible without anyone deliberately making them visible. The key difference from the other meanings: nothing is being shown to anyone in particular; it simply becomes apparent.

  • The stain shows through the shirt. (You can see it; it's noticeable.)
  • Her age is starting to show. (It's becoming evident.)
  • It shows on your face. (It's plainly visible.)
  • Hard work shows. (The results are evident to others.)

7. To escort or guide someone to a place

This meaning is about physically taking or leading someone somewhere, usually as a host or guide.

  • The hotel staff showed us to our room. (Led us there personally.)
  • She showed him into the office. (Opened the door and led him in.)
  • He showed us around the factory. (Gave us a guided tour.)

This is a polite, hospitable use. The person doing the "showing" takes you somewhere rather than just pointing.

8. To screen or exhibit publicly

When a film, artwork, or exhibition is displayed to an audience, it is said to be "shown."

  • The cinema is showing a new film tonight. (Screening/playing it.)
  • The gallery is showing her paintings. (Exhibiting them.)
  • They showed the documentary at the festival.

9. To display a reading or value (instruments and devices)

Meters, clocks, dials, screens, and similar instruments "show" a value when they display or register it.

  • The thermometer shows 38 degrees.
  • The screen shows an error message.
  • Her GPS showed that she was going the wrong way.

10. To arrive or appear (informal)

In informal use, especially in American English, "show" means to arrive or appear somewhere. ("Show up" is the more common full form, but "show" alone is also used.)

  • He never showed. (He never arrived.)
  • She finally showed at noon.
How to Use It in a Sentence

"Show" is a ditransitive verb — it typically takes two objects: the person who is shown, and the thing being shown.

Pattern 1 — show + person + thing (more common in speech)

  • She showed me her photos.
  • He showed us the problem.

Pattern 2 — show + thing + to + person

  • She showed her photos to me.
  • He showed the problem to us.

Pattern 3 — show + that + clause (to demonstrate or prove)

  • The evidence shows that the company was wrong.
  • He showed that the story was false.

Pattern 4 — show + person + how / where / when / why

  • Can you show me how to do this?
  • She showed him where to put the boxes.

Past tense: showed
Past participle: shown (standard) — or showed (informal, especially American English)

  • He has shown great courage. (standard)
  • She was shown the door. (passive — she was told/made to leave)

Show off — to display something (or yourself) in order to impress others; to boast through action rather than words.

  • He was showing off his new car.
  • Stop showing off!

Show up — has three distinct meanings:

  1. To arrive or appear: She finally showed up at noon.
  2. To make someone look bad by comparison: He showed everyone up by finishing first.
  3. To become visible: The dirt shows up against the white fabric.

Show around — to give someone a tour of a place.

  • Let me show you around the office.

Show in / Show out — to escort someone in or out of a place.

  • Please show Mr. Smith in. (Lead him here from the door.)
  • He showed the guests out. (Led them to the exit.)

Have something to show for — to have a visible, tangible result from your effort.

  • He worked for hours and had nothing to show for it.

Show your hand — (from card games) to reveal your intentions, plans, or secrets.

  • Don't show your hand too early in negotiations.

Show your face — to appear somewhere, especially after a long absence or something embarrassing.

  • After that incident, he was afraid to show his face in the office.

Show willing — (British English) to demonstrate that you are ready and cooperative, even if you're not enthusiastic.

  • Even if you don't enjoy it, show willing.

Show the way — to lead by example; to be the first to do something that others can follow.

  • She showed the way by investing in renewable energy.

It shows — used to say that something is clearly noticeable. Usually a compliment or a neutral observation that something internal has become externally visible.

  • "Did you practice a lot?" "Yes, and it shows."
  • "He tries to hide his nervousness, but it shows."

Show of hands — when people raise their hand to vote or signal agreement.

  • Can I see a show of hands — who agrees?

Show someone the door — to tell someone to leave; to dismiss them.

  • When he kept arguing, the manager showed him the door.

Show someone the ropes — to teach a newcomer how things work.

  • Her first week at work, her colleague showed her the ropes.

Show vs. Tell

One of the most important distinctions in English. To tell is to inform someone using words. To show is to make something evident through action, evidence, or demonstration.

  • He told me he was brave. — He said the words "I am brave."
  • He showed me he was brave. — His actions made his bravery evident.

Telling is easy; showing requires proof. This is why "actions speak louder than words" — showing is more convincing than telling.

Show vs. Prove

"Show" and "prove" overlap when "show" means to demonstrate with evidence, but "prove" is stronger and more absolute — it implies leaving no doubt. "Show" suggests the evidence makes something clear, without necessarily eliminating every last doubt. "Prove" closes the door entirely.

"Show" and evidence

When "show" is used with data, research, or numbers — the study shows, the figures show, the results show — it carries authoritative weight. It implies the evidence itself speaks clearly, not that someone is merely guessing. "The data shows X" is a stronger claim than "the data suggests X."

"It shows" — a small phrase worth knowing well

When someone says it shows, they mean that something internal (effort, emotion, experience, quality) has become externally visible — often without the person intending it, or as a natural result.

  • "You've been working hard on this." "Yes, and it shows." — Your effort is visible in the results.
  • "He's trying to hide his anger, but it shows." — It's noticeable despite his attempt to hide it.

It's often a compliment. If someone says "your dedication shows," they mean your dedication is plainly evident to anyone who looks.

Whether you are showing someone your passport, showing courage, showing someone to their seat, showing that a theory is wrong, or noticing that the tiredness is starting to show on someone's face — the single thread running through every meaning is this:

Something that was not yet seen, known, or evident is now made perceptible.

That is "show," in full.
14551:
To showcase something means to present or display it in a way that deliberately highlights its best, most impressive qualities — so that others notice, appreciate, or admire it.

It's not just showing. It's showing strategically, with the goal of making something look its best.
The key idea: intention + favorable display

The heart of this word is deliberate intent. When you showcase something, you are consciously putting it forward so it gets noticed and appreciated.

Think of it like this: if you simply show someone a painting, you hold it up and say "here it is." But if you showcase a painting, you hang it in perfect lighting, frame it beautifully, and position it so the viewer's eye is drawn to its finest details. The goal is to impress.

This deliberate effort is always present in "showcase." Nothing is accidentally showcased — there is always someone or something doing the work of presenting it favorably.
How it differs from similar words

Show is neutral. It just makes something visible.
"I showed him the report." — No special effort to impress. Just handing it over.

Display is also fairly neutral — arranging things so they can be seen.
"The items were displayed on the shelf." — No strong suggestion of highlighting strengths.

Showcase goes further. It carries the idea of deliberately drawing attention to strengths, with an audience in mind.
"The exhibition showcased her finest work." — Carefully chosen, carefully presented, with the goal of impressing the viewer.

Flaunt is about showing something off in a boastful, often excessive way — it usually has a negative or arrogant feel. Showcase, by contrast, is positive and professional in tone.

Showcase almost always puts something in a favorable light. It is used to highlight what is good, strong, impressive, or admirable about something.

You would not naturally say "the report showcased his mistakes" in straightforward speech — that would sound ironic or sarcastic, because the word itself implies something worth admiring. When someone uses it that way, they are being deliberately ironic.

A wide range of things can be showcased:

  • Talent or ability — a concert that showcases young musicians
  • Skills or expertise — a job interview where you showcase your problem-solving skills
  • Work or achievements — a portfolio that showcases your best projects
  • Products or services — a company showcasing its latest product at a trade fair
  • People — a director who uses a film to showcase an unknown actor
  • Qualities or features — a speech that showcases someone's intelligence and leadership
  • Places or natural wonders — a documentary that showcases the biodiversity of a rainforest
Who or what can "do" the showcasing?

Both people and things can serve as the subject of this verb.

A person can showcase their own talent — "She showcased her skills during the presentation."

An event or platform can showcase something — "The festival showcases independent filmmakers."

A work (a film, a book, a speech) can showcase something — "The film showcases his remarkable range as an actor."

A product, place, or exhibition can showcase features — "The expo showcases the latest developments in renewable energy."

1. The annual science fair was organized to showcase student innovation.
  2. She used her cover letter to showcase her most relevant accomplishments.
  3. The company will showcase its new software at the conference next month.
  4. The documentary beautifully showcases the wildlife of the Serengeti.
  5. His final performance truly showcased how much he had grown as a musician.
  6. The gallery was designed specifically to showcase emerging artists from the region.
  7. The championship game showcased everything that makes this team exceptional.
  8. He created a personal website to showcase his photography to potential clients.
An important nuance: "showcase" is always transitive

As a verb, showcase always needs an object — you must showcase something. You cannot simply "showcase" without saying what is being showcased.

✅ "The event will showcase local talent."
❌ "The event will showcase." — This is incomplete and unnatural.
Where you will commonly encounter this word

• Business and marketing — companies showcasing products or services
  • Arts and entertainment — films, concerts, and exhibitions showcasing creative work
  • Career contexts — resumes, portfolios, and interviews used to showcase achievements
  • Sports — athletes or teams showcasing abilities in a performance
  • Education — events that showcase student projects or creative work
  • Journalism and media — articles or documentaries that showcase a subject favorably

To showcase = to present something in the best possible light, with the deliberate goal of impressing or gaining the appreciation of an audience.

It is intentional, it is favorable, and it is about putting the best version of something in front of people who matter.
14552: Showmanship is the skill of presenting something — yourself, your talent, or your work — in a way that is exciting, dramatic, and entertaining. It's not just what you do, but how you do it in front of others, in a way that makes them pay attention, feel impressed, and remember it.

Think of two musicians who are equally talented. One walks on stage, plays their songs perfectly, and walks off. The other walks on stage with incredible energy, connects with every single person in the crowd, builds moments of suspense, knows exactly when to be quiet and when to explode, and leaves the audience on their feet. Both played the same music. Only the second one had showmanship.

That's the heart of it. Showmanship is the craft of making a moment feel special for an audience. It lives in the gap between simply doing something and performing it.

Showmanship is made up of several things working together. It involves timing — knowing the perfect moment to reveal something, pause for effect, or build suspense. It involves confidence — carrying yourself in a way that says "watch this" without saying a word. It involves reading your audience — sensing what they want, what will excite them, and giving it to them at exactly the right moment. And it involves a certain theatrical flair — a natural or practiced ability to make ordinary actions feel grand and memorable.

A magician who pulls out a coin and makes it disappear is doing a trick. A magician who leans in close, looks you in the eye, builds the anticipation, makes the coin vanish, then produces it from behind your ear while the whole room gasps — that's showmanship. The trick is the same. The experience is completely different.
Where you'll see this word used:

Showmanship is most commonly used in the world of entertainment — sports, music, theater, magic, comedy, and circus performance. You might hear, "His guitar playing was good, but it was his showmanship that won the crowd over." It's also used in business, where a brilliant product launch with dramatic reveals and storytelling is praised as great showmanship (think of the late Steve Jobs presenting a new Apple product). Even in cooking competitions, a chef who plates a dish in a theatrical, visually stunning way is displaying showmanship.

The word can also be used in everyday contexts. A teacher who makes lessons dramatic and memorable, a coach who fires up a team with an unforgettable speech, or a salesperson who presents their pitch with energy and charisma — all of these can be described as showing showmanship.
The nuance — when it's a compliment and when it's a mild criticism:

Most of the time, showmanship is a compliment. Saying someone has "great showmanship" means they have a rare and valued ability to captivate people.

However, sometimes it carries a subtle warning. If someone says a performance was "all showmanship and no substance," they mean the person was flashy and entertaining but lacked real depth or skill underneath. In this sense, showmanship alone — without genuine talent or content to back it up — can be seen as hollow. Think of a politician who gives electrifying speeches but has no real ideas, or a performer who dazzles visually but can't actually sing. So the word can sometimes hint that style is covering for a lack of real substance, though this negative shade only appears when the context makes it clear.

The pure, positive meaning is far more common. Showmanship, at its best, means someone has both the talent and the ability to present that talent in the most powerful, memorable way possible.
A helpful way to remember it:

A showman is a person who performs and entertains with great style. Showmanship is the quality that makes them a showman — their mastery of the art of putting on a show. So whenever you see the word, ask yourself: Is this person simply doing something, or are they performing it in a way that makes an audience feel something? That feeling — and the skill required to create it — is showmanship.
14553: Shrapnel is the jagged, sharp fragments of metal — and sometimes other hard materials — that fly outward at deadly speed when something explodes.

Imagine a metal grenade sitting on the ground. When it explodes, it doesn't just produce a ball of fire and a loud bang. The metal shell of the grenade itself shatters into dozens or hundreds of small, irregular, razor-sharp pieces. Those pieces are shrapnel. They shoot outward in all directions, like a burst of tiny, lethal bullets — except far more unpredictable in shape and direction.

Shrapnel comes from explosive devices. The most common sources are:

  • Bombs and artillery shells — the outer metal casing breaks apart during the explosion
  • Grenades — the metal body fragments into jagged pieces
  • Landmines — the explosion sends metal fragments flying upward and outward
  • IEDs (Improvised Explosive Devices) — homemade bombs that sometimes have nails, bolts, or ball bearings packed inside specifically to increase the amount of shrapnel
  • Any exploding machinery or object — a boiler, a car engine, a gas canister — if it explodes, the pieces that fly off are called shrapnel

The key is that shrapnel is always a byproduct of an explosion. Without the explosion, there is no shrapnel.

Shrapnel has no fixed, uniform shape — that's what makes it particularly dangerous. A single explosion can produce:

  • Tiny slivers the size of a grain of rice
  • Coin-sized jagged chunks
  • Long, blade-like strips of metal
  • Irregular, asymmetric fragments that look like broken puzzle pieces with sharp edges

They are almost never smooth or round. Their edges tend to be jagged, rough, and uneven, like the edge of torn metal — because that is exactly what they are.

Three things make shrapnel especially deadly:

  1. Speed: The explosive force launches fragments at extremely high velocity — often faster than a bullet. At that speed, even a small piece of metal can pass through skin, muscle, and bone.
  2. Unpredictability: Unlike a bullet, which travels in one direction, shrapnel from a single explosion can fly in hundreds of different directions at once, hitting multiple people or hitting one person in multiple places simultaneously.
  3. Invisibility inside the body: Shrapnel pieces are often small enough to lodge deep inside a wound without being immediately visible. A person can be hit by shrapnel and not even feel every piece at first, only to suffer serious internal damage.

Shrapnel wounds are among the most common injuries in warfare and terrorist attacks. When a fragment enters the body, it can:

  • Tear through muscle and tissue
  • Puncture organs
  • Damage blood vessels, causing internal bleeding
  • Splinter into even smaller pieces inside the body upon impact

Surgeons who treat shrapnel victims often have to remove the fragments manually, which is a delicate process because pieces can be lodged near nerves, arteries, or the spine. In some cases, if a fragment is too close to a critical structure, doctors leave it in the body permanently, as removing it would cause more harm than leaving it. Soldiers and civilians who survive such injuries sometimes carry shrapnel inside their bodies for the rest of their lives.

The word has expanded beyond the battlefield. In general usage, people use "shrapnel" to refer to any sharp debris flung outward by an explosion or violent rupture, even in non-military situations. For example:

  • If a pressure cooker explodes in a kitchen, the flying metal pieces are called shrapnel.
  • If a car tyre bursts at high speed and pieces of rubber and metal fly off, those are sometimes called shrapnel.
  • If a firework malfunctions and scatters debris, that debris is shrapnel.

The common thread across all these uses is the same: fragments + explosion + dangerous outward force = shrapnel.
One informal slang use (British and Australian English)

In casual British and Australian slang, "shrapnel" is also used humorously to mean small loose coins — the kind that accumulates annoyingly at the bottom of your pocket or bag. The idea is that small coins are scattered, numerous, and a bit of a nuisance, just like actual shrapnel. This usage is entirely informal and lighthearted, and is unrelated to the serious, literal meaning.

If you want one clean image to anchor this word in your memory: picture a metal grenade exploding in slow motion. The shell breaks apart. Dozens of sharp, irregular metal pieces fly outward in all directions at tremendous speed. Those pieces — right there — are shrapnel.
14554: The word shrew has two distinct meanings. One refers to a real animal, and the other refers to a type of person. Both are important and worth knowing well.

A shrew is a tiny, fur-covered mammal that looks very much like a mouse. However, it is not a rodent — it is actually a completely different kind of creature, more closely related to moles. It has a long, pointed snout (nose), very small eyes, and velvety fur.

What makes shrews remarkable:

Shrews are among the most energetic animals on Earth. Their hearts beat at an astonishing rate — sometimes over 1,000 times per minute — and their bodies burn through energy so fast that they must eat almost constantly. A shrew that goes without food for even a few hours can starve to death. To survive, it eats insects, worms, seeds, and sometimes even small animals larger than itself.

Shrews are found on almost every continent and live in forests, grasslands, and gardens. They are small enough to fit in the palm of your hand, yet they are fierce, aggressive hunters. Some species even have a mild venom in their saliva, which they use to paralyze small prey.

Because of their frantic lifestyle and intense, nervous energy, shrews have a reputation for being agitated, restless creatures.

In its second meaning, a shrew refers to a person — traditionally a woman — who is bad-tempered, sharp-tongued, constantly scolding, and difficult to deal with. A shrew is someone who nags, complains loudly, argues aggressively, and creates conflict around them.

This meaning is connected to the animal: just as the animal is known for being fierce and agitated, a person called a shrew is seen as temperamentally hostile and combative.

How it is used:

If someone describes a character in a story as "a shrew," they mean she is the kind of person who snaps at people, picks fights easily, and has a harsh, unpleasant manner. For example:

  • "The landlady was a shrew — she shouted at tenants over the smallest things."
  • "Her neighbors avoided her because she was known as the local shrew."

Important note on this usage:

This meaning is old-fashioned and is today considered offensive and sexist, because it has historically been applied almost exclusively to women as a way to dismiss or belittle them. In modern writing and speech, calling a woman a shrew is seen as a derogatory insult. You will, however, encounter it frequently in older literature, most famously in William Shakespeare's play The Taming of the Shrew, which is entirely built around this idea.

Being aware of this word in its literary and historical sense is essential for reading classic English literature, even if you would never use it to describe a real person today.

The connection between the animal and the insult is deliberate. The shrew-animal is known for being highly strung, aggressive, and constantly making noise. People who coined the insult were drawing a comparison: calling someone a shrew was saying they had the same frantic, biting, irritable nature as the animal. This kind of word — where an animal's traits are mapped onto human behavior — is very common in English (think: "snake," "wolf," "viper").

As an animalA tiny, fierce, fast-moving mammal with a pointed snout; eats constantly; highly energetic
As a personA quarrelsome, sharp-tongued, bad-tempered person (historically applied to women; now considered offensive)

Both meanings share the same core idea: intense, aggressive, agitated energy — whether in a creature or a character.
14555:
A shrewd person is someone who is practically clever in a sharp, perceptive way — especially when it comes to understanding people, situations, and how to get the best outcome for themselves.

Think of a shrewd person as someone who sees through things. They aren't easily fooled. They notice what others miss. They think a few steps ahead. And they apply all of this to make smart, calculated decisions — particularly in competitive or complex situations like business, negotiations, or dealing with tricky people.

This is important to understand, because many learners assume shrewd simply means intelligent or clever. It doesn't — not exactly.

"Smart" and "clever" are broad words that describe someone who learns quickly or solves problems well. Shrewd is more specific and more powerful than either. A shrewd person isn't just generally intelligent. They have a particular kind of intelligence: the ability to accurately read a situation, understand what's really happening beneath the surface, and then act on that understanding to their advantage.

Here's a simple illustration. A clever student learns the material quickly. A shrewd student does that and quietly figures out exactly what the teacher is likely to test, and prepares precisely for those points. The shrewd person always asks themselves: "What's really going on here? What do people actually want? What's the smartest move I can make right now?"
The Subtle Tone: Respect with a Faint Edge

This is a nuance you must understand to truly own this word.

Shrewd is mostly a positive or neutral word. When you call someone shrewd, you're genuinely respecting them — you're saying they're impressively sharp and practical. But there's a faint implication that their cleverness is directed toward their own advantage, not necessarily for everyone's benefit equally. A shrewd person is looking out for themselves, and they're very good at it.

This is what separates shrewd from the word wise. A wise person's intelligence tends to be deep, balanced, and often moral — their insight benefits everyone around them. A shrewd person's intelligence is more tactical and self-focused. They're good at winning. You'd go to a wise person for meaningful life guidance. You'd want a shrewd person firmly on your side in a tough negotiation.

Cunning is shrewd's darker cousin, and the difference matters.

A cunning person achieves their goals through trickery, manipulation, and deception. Shrewd doesn't go that far. A shrewd person is sharp and self-interested, but not necessarily dishonest. They might get a great deal through clever, perceptive negotiation — not through lying or manipulation. The moment a shrewd person starts deceiving people, we'd shift to calling them cunning, or perhaps sly. So: shrewd sits comfortably between "impressively clever" and "manipulative," leaning toward the positive side.
What Shrewd Looks Like in Real Life

In business, a shrewd businessperson spots an opportunity others haven't noticed, buys at the right moment, and exits at the right moment too. They're not impulsive — they observe carefully, think it through, and then act decisively. They understand what the market actually values, not just what people say it does.

In negotiations, a shrewd negotiator understands what the other side truly wants — beneath what they're openly saying. They use this insight to quietly structure a deal that appears balanced but subtly favors them.

In reading people, a shrewd judge of character can quickly determine someone's real motives, values, and reliability — simply by observing how they speak, what they choose to talk about, and how they behave under pressure.

In investing, a shrewd investment is one where you recognized the real value of something before others did — and you acted on that recognition at the right time.
How the Word Is Actually Used in Sentences

Here are authentic examples of how you'll encounter this word in the wild:

"She's a shrewd businesswoman who never signs a contract without reading every line."

"That was a shrewd move — he sold his shares right before the market crashed."

"He's a shrewd observer of human nature; he reads people almost instantly."

"Despite her quiet manner, she's remarkably shrewd — she notices absolutely everything."

"The company made a shrewd decision to expand into new markets before its competitors even considered it."

Notice the pattern: shrewd is used to describe a person (a shrewd politician, investor, negotiator), a decision or action (a shrewd move, a shrewd investment, a shrewd choice), or a mental quality (shrewd judgment, shrewd observation, shrewd thinking).

Shrewdly is the adverb form: "She shrewdly avoided committing to anything until she had gathered all the facts."

Shrewdness is the noun form: "His shrewdness in business dealings made him wealthy before he turned forty."

You can also intensify the adjective naturally — quite shrewd, very shrewd, extremely shrewd, remarkably shrewd — all of these work and are common.
One Final Image to Lock It In

Picture someone sitting quietly in a room full of people. While everyone else is talking and reacting to what's happening on the surface, this person is calmly watching — noticing the small things, reading people's real intentions, understanding the invisible patterns. When they finally speak or act, it's precise, well-timed, and almost always to their benefit.

That person is shrewd.

If someone ever calls you shrewd, take it as a genuine compliment. They're saying you're impressively sharp, perceptive, and practically intelligent. The only tiny asterisk is that they probably also mean you're very good at looking out for yourself — which, depending on the situation, is no bad thing at all.
14556:
When you do something shrewdly, you do it with sharp, practical intelligence — in a way that shows you clearly understand a situation, see what others might miss, and use that understanding to your advantage.

It is the adverb form of the adjective shrewd, which describes a person with this quality. So a shrewd person thinks this way; a person who acts shrewdly is acting on that thinking.

Imagine a chess player who, in just a few seconds, spots a hidden trap in the game that nobody else sees — and makes a move that turns everything in their favour. That player acted shrewdly.

Shrewdness is not about being book-smart or showing off your knowledge. It is about reading a situation accurately and making the smartest practical move — especially under real-world conditions like money, negotiation, business, or dealing with people.

When someone acts shrewdly, three things are usually true:

  1. They see clearly. They understand what is really happening — not just what appears to be happening on the surface.
  2. They think fast and sharp. They process the situation quickly and make a sound judgment.
  3. They act to their benefit. The result of their action is usually a smart gain — financial, strategic, or social.

"Shrewdly" carries a tone of quiet, almost effortless cleverness. It suggests someone who is not making noise about how smart they are — they are simply being smart in a way that gets results.

It is mostly a positive or neutral word. When you say someone acted shrewdly, you are usually admiring their sharpness. However, in some contexts, it can carry a very slight edge of cunning — meaning the person is clever in a self-serving, calculating way. But it does not mean dishonest or unethical. A shrewd person bends the game in their favour within the rules.
How It Differs from Similar Words

This is important, because "shrewdly" is often confused with similar-sounding words:

  • Wisely → Wisdom is broad and moral. A wise person makes decisions based on deep experience and good values. Shrewdness is narrower — it is about practical sharpness, not moral depth. You can act shrewdly without being wise, and wisely without being shrewd.
  • Cleverly → Cleverness is about ingenuity and creative problem-solving — finding a smart trick or a novel solution. Shrewdness is more about reading situations and people accurately. A clever magician invents a new trick; a shrewd businessperson spots a deal others overlooked.
  • Intelligently → Intelligence refers to raw thinking power. Shrewdness is a specific application of intelligence — in practical, real-world judgment. A very intelligent person might still fail to act shrewdly if they cannot read people or situations well.
  • Cunningly → Cunning implies slyness or craftiness, often with a deceptive or slightly sneaky quality. Shrewdly is cleaner than this — it does not necessarily imply any trickery.

Shrewdly appears most naturally in contexts involving:

Business and money:

"She shrewdly bought the property before property prices in that area rose."
Here, she anticipated what others did not and acted on it. The result was financial gain.

Negotiations:

"He shrewdly agreed to the small concession, knowing it would make the other side feel like they had won — while he kept the bigger prize."
He gave up something minor to secure something major. That is shrewd negotiation.

Reading people:

"She shrewdly noticed that the salesman was being unusually enthusiastic, which meant the product probably had hidden problems."
Most people would be distracted by the enthusiasm. She saw through it.

Strategy (politics, military, sports):

"The coach shrewdly rested his best player in the early rounds, saving him for the final."
A short-term sacrifice for a long-term win — classic shrewd thinking.

Investments:

"They shrewdly invested in that small tech company when it was unknown — it became one of the biggest in the world."
A Picture to Remember It By

Think of a street-smart merchant at a busy market. He is not a professor. He has not read many books. But the moment someone walks up to his stall, he instantly reads whether they are a serious buyer or just browsing, what price they are willing to pay, and how to present his goods to get the best deal. He acts on all of this in real time, quietly and efficiently.

That merchant is acting shrewdly — not because he is showing off intelligence, but because he is applying sharp, practical judgment to get the best outcome.
Shrewdly = in a way that is sharp, practically clever, and perceptive — especially in understanding real-world situations, people, or opportunities, and acting on them to one's advantage.
14557:
To shriek means to make a very loud, high-pitched, sharp cry or sound that bursts out suddenly and involuntarily. It's not just any loud sound — it has a specific quality: high in pitch, piercing (meaning it cuts sharply through other sounds), and uncontrolled.

Think of the sound a person makes when something suddenly scares them — that instant, sharp, high sound that escapes before they even decide to make it. That's a shriek.
The two key qualities that define shrieking

Understanding these two qualities will help you recognize and use the word correctly:

1. High-pitched — A shriek is never a deep or low sound. It's sharp and high, the kind of sound that goes straight to your ears.

2. Involuntary and uncontrolled — This is crucial. People don't choose to shriek the way they choose to speak. It bursts out of them, driven by overwhelming emotion. This sense of losing control is built into the word.

Shrieking is triggered by extreme emotions — the kind that are so powerful that the sound simply escapes a person:

  • Sudden fear or terror — This is the most classic use. Someone sees something frightening, and they shriek.
  • Sudden shock or surprise — Even something unexpected (not necessarily scary) can cause a shriek.
  • Extreme pain — A sharp, sudden pain can make someone shriek.
  • Extreme excitement or delight — Children very commonly shriek when they're wildly excited. The same high-pitched, uncontrolled quality appears here too.
  • Uncontrolled laughter — The phrase "shrieked with laughter" is very common. It means laughing so hard and freely that your laughter becomes high-pitched and unrestrained.

People shriek most commonly. But the word goes beyond humans:

  • Animals — Birds, monkeys, and certain other animals shriek. A bird of prey, for example, can shriek.
  • Wind — Writers often say the wind shrieks during a fierce storm. This is a creative use, giving the wind a human-like quality, and it perfectly captures that sharp, high-pitched howl of a strong wind.
  • Machines or objects — Brakes, tyres, or metal surfaces can shriek — meaning they produce that same sharp, piercing, high-pitched sound.
How to use it in a sentence

Intransitive (shrieking without saying words):

  • She shrieked when the dog jumped at her.
  • The children shrieked with excitement at the carnival.
  • He shrieked in pain and dropped the knife.

Transitive (shrieking actual words out):

  • "Get out!" she shrieked.
  • She shrieked his name across the hallway.
  • "Run!" he shrieked as the wall collapsed.

With "with" (to describe the emotion driving the shriek):

  • shriek with fear
  • shriek with laughter
  • shriek with delight
  • shriek with excitement

"At" someone (directed shrieking, often out of anger or panic):

  • She shrieked at him to stop the car.
  • The crowd shrieked at the performer.
How shriek is different from similar words

This is important, because words like scream, yell, and cry are close — but not identical:

Shriek vs. Scream:
These are the most similar. The difference is subtle but real. A scream can be deep or high-pitched, and it can be long and sustained. A shriek is specifically high-pitched and tends to be sharper and more sudden — like a single piercing burst. You can imagine a prolonged scream of terror, but a shriek is more like an explosive moment of sound.

Shriek vs. Yell/Shout:
Yelling and shouting are loud, but they are deliberate and controlled. You choose to yell at someone. You never really "choose" to shriek — it's involuntary. Also, yelling is usually not high-pitched; shrieking always is.

Shriek vs. Cry:
"Cry" is a very broad word — it can mean weeping, or any kind of calling out. Shrieking is a specific, high-pitched, piercing burst. All shrieks could loosely be called cries, but most cries are not shrieks.

Shriek vs. Squeal:
A squeal is also high-pitched and uncontrolled, but it's lighter and often associated with milder emotions — a little surprise, mild excitement, playful delight. A shriek is more intense, more forceful, and suggests a stronger emotional charge.

Shriek vs. Wail:
A wail is a prolonged, mournful cry — lower, sustained, associated with grief and sorrow. A shriek is sharp and sudden. The two are very different in character.

When you read or hear the word shriek, it creates an immediate sensory impact. It is vivid and expressive. Good writers choose this word precisely because it communicates not just that a sound was made, but what kind of sound — sharp, high, forceful, out of control. It makes the reader almost hear the sound.

It is a word that belongs to moments of intensity. Wherever you see it, something strong is happening — fear, shock, wild laughter, unbearable pain, overwhelming joy.
A quick summary to anchor everything

To shriek = to make a sudden, loud, high-pitched, piercing sound driven by overwhelming emotion — a sound that is not controlled or chosen, but simply escapes.

The emotion is usually extreme: terror, sudden shock, sharp pain, wild excitement, or helpless laughter. The sound is never deep or low. It is always sharp, high, and piercing. Humans shriek, some animals shriek, and even wind and machines are described as shrieking when they produce that same sharp, high, cutting sound.
14558: Shrill describes a sound that is very high in pitch, sharp, and unpleasantly piercing — the kind that hits your ears in a way that makes you wince. Think of a fire alarm blaring in a small room, a child screaming at the top of their lungs, a referee blowing hard into a whistle, or a car alarm cutting through the night. These are shrill sounds. They demand your attention not because they are pleasant, but because they are sharp, cutting, and impossible to ignore.

This is the most important thing to understand. Not every high-pitched sound is shrill. A flute playing softly is high-pitched, but warm and gentle. A woman humming a lullaby can be high-pitched but soothing. Shrill adds something extra on top of high pitch — a harsh, penetrating, grating quality that makes the sound feel like it is stabbing through everything else around it. So the full formula is: high-pitched plus unpleasantly sharp and piercing.

The figurative meaning — and this is where the word gets really interesting

Shrill is not only used for sounds. It is also used to describe how a person speaks, argues, or makes demands — and this extended meaning is extremely common in everyday English.

When a person, a voice, or an argument is called shrill, it means the expression is so forceful, so emotionally intense, and so insistent that it becomes unpleasant and even counterproductive. It suggests someone has pushed past the point of being persuasive and has crossed into being grating, over-the-top, or frantic. For example, "The politician's shrill warnings about the economy made people uncomfortable" means the warnings were delivered with such sharp, relentless urgency that they felt excessive. Or, "As the argument went on, her tone became shrill" means her voice and manner became harsh and piercing in a way that was difficult to listen to calmly.

In this figurative sense, calling something shrill is almost always a criticism. It implies a loss of composure, a lack of nuance, or an emotional intensity so high that it actually pushes people away rather than drawing them in.
The attitude this word carries — its connotation

Shrill is nearly always negative, whether it describes a sound or a person's manner. It never suggests something admirable. A shrill voice is not just high — it is uncomfortable. A shrill argument is not just passionate — it is excessive and unpleasant. The word carries a sense of too much: too loud, too sharp, too intense, too piercing.

In real-world usage, the word "shrill" has sometimes been applied unfairly and disproportionately to women — particularly when they argue or express strong opinions. A woman speaking passionately may be called "shrill," while a man doing the exact same thing might simply be called "assertive" or "forceful." Many people are aware of this bias and point it out as an example of unequal treatment. Being aware of this will help you understand the word's full weight when you encounter it in writing or conversation, and it will help you use it thoughtfully yourself.
Piercing, screeching, strident, and ear-splitting all share territory with shrill. The best near-synonym is strident, which also means unpleasantly loud and insistent, especially in tone or manner.
Mellow, deep, dulcet, soft, and gentle are antonyms. A mellow sound is warm and low; a shrill sound is sharp and high. Thinking of these opposites helps you feel the full distance the word covers.
A few example sentences to make it stick

"The shrill whistle of the kettle cut through every conversation in the house." Here, it is purely about sound — high-pitched and piercing. "The debate quickly turned shrill, with both sides yelling rather than reasoning." Here, it is figurative — the argument became harsh and unpleasant. "She heard a shrill scream from the next room and ran to check." This combines both senses — the scream is literally high-pitched and sharp, and also alarming and hard to ignore.

The word is versatile, but its heart is always the same idea: something sharp, cutting, and high that bothers you — whether in your ears or in your mind.
14559:
To shrive means to hear someone's confession of sins, give them a task of penance (something they must do to show true regret), and then formally forgive them — all as an act of religious authority. It is rooted in the Christian practice of sacramental confession, and the word is almost always used in a religious or historical context.

It is an old, literary word. You will not hear it in everyday modern speech, but you will encounter it in older literature, religious writing, and in one very famous cultural expression: Shrove Tuesday.
The Two Sides of the Word

This verb has an interesting quality: it can describe the action from two different points of view, and both are correct uses of the word.

1. When the priest shrives someone:
The priest is the one doing the shriving. He listens to the confession, assigns a penance, and pronounces absolution (forgiveness). In this sense, to shrive is something a priest does to a penitent.

"The old friar shrove the dying soldier before the battle."

2. When a person goes to be shriven:
The ordinary person — the sinner seeking forgiveness — goes to the priest to be shriven. Here, the person is on the receiving end of the act. They confess, they accept penance, they receive forgiveness, and they are now shriven — cleansed of their sins through this formal process.

"She knelt and begged to be shriven before she died."

Both uses are correct and natural, just describing the same event from opposite angles.
The Three Steps That Make Up "Shriving"

To fully understand the word, you need to understand what actually happens during the act of shriving. It is not just one thing — it is a three-part process:

Step 1 — Confession:
The penitent (the person seeking forgiveness) openly admits their sins to the priest. This act of confession is considered essential; you cannot be shriven without honestly declaring what you have done wrong.

Step 2 — Penance:
The priest assigns a penance — a specific act the person must perform to demonstrate genuine sorrow and a desire to make amends. This could be a set of prayers, a charitable act, or some form of self-discipline. It is the outward sign of inner repentance.

Step 3 — Absolution:
The priest formally pronounces that the person's sins are forgiven, speaking in the authority of God (in Catholic and certain other Christian traditions). This is the official release from the burden of those sins.

To shrive someone is to carry out this entire process with them. To be shriven is to have gone through it and emerged forgiven.
Key Verb Forms You Need to Know

Because this word is old, its forms are irregular — and they appear in real-world usage, so you should know them:

  • Shrive — the base form (present tense): "I must shrive you before you go."
  • Shrove — the simple past tense: "The priest shrove him that very evening."
  • Shriven — the past participle (used with "have" or "be"): "He had not been shriven in twenty years."

The past participle shriven is probably the form you will encounter most often in literature and older texts.
Shrove Tuesday — The Word's Most Famous Survival

The clearest trace of this word in modern life is Shrove Tuesday, the day before Ash Wednesday (the beginning of Lent in the Christian calendar). The name literally comes from "shrove" — the past tense of shrive.

On this day, Christians were traditionally expected to go to confession — to be shriven — before the solemn fasting season of Lent began. It was a day of spiritual cleansing and preparation. This is also why Shrove Tuesday is known as Pancake Day in the UK and parts of the world: people would use up rich ingredients (eggs, butter, milk) before the fasting of Lent started. The religious act and the culinary tradition grew up together around the same day.

So whenever you hear "Shrove Tuesday," you are hearing a fossil of the verb to shrive, frozen in time.

Occasionally, writers use "shrive" in a loosely figurative sense — to mean any act of unburdening oneself of guilt, seeking forgiveness, or receiving a kind of emotional absolution, even outside a strictly religious context. For example, a character in a novel might confess a terrible secret to a friend and feel "shriven" afterward — meaning spiritually lighter, as if forgiven. This is a poetic extension of the word's core meaning and works because the emotional experience of confession and forgiveness is universal, even when the religious machinery is not present.

However, this figurative use is not the word's primary meaning. Its heart is always the formal, priestly act of sacramental confession.
Who Uses This Word, and Where?

This is an archaic and literary word. It belongs to:

  • Religious and historical writing about medieval or early modern Christian practice
  • Classic literature — Shakespeare, Chaucer, and other older writers use it naturally
  • Poetry — especially poetry dealing with sin, guilt, death, and redemption
  • Modern writing that wants to invoke a medieval or deeply religious tone

You will not hear it in a normal conversation today. But when you encounter it in a text, you will now know exactly what is happening: someone is confessing, receiving penance, and being forgiven — or a priest is presiding over that sacred exchange.
A Final Summary in One Sentence
To shrive is to formally hear a person's confession of sins, assign them a penance, and grant them absolution — and to be shriven is to have gone through that entire process and emerged forgiven.
